analysis.one_liner: Repeals limits on physician-owned hospitals and rules requiring drug and device makers to disclose payments to doctors.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by one Republican sponsor and five cosponsors, never got a committee vote and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2010 health care law did two things this bill would undo: it generally stopped physicians from referring Medicare patients to hospitals they own a piece of, and it required drug and device companies to publicly report payments and gifts to doctors and their ownership stakes in those companies. This bill would erase both rules and restore the older law, retroactive to the day the health care law passed. It was referred to two House committees, sent to a health subcommittee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians who own stakes in specialty hospitals, such as heart and surgical hospitals, would again be able to expand those facilities and refer their Medicare patients to them. Drug, device, biological, and medical supply manufacturers would no longer have to report payments to physicians or disclose physician ownership to the Health and Human Services Department.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Physician-owned hospital investors and device makers

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the health care law's limits on the Medicare exception to the physician self-referral ban, which had barred hospitals without a Medicare provider agreement by August 1, 2010 from participating in Medicare except under narrow rural exceptions.

It repeals the requirement that drug, device, biological, and medical supply manufacturers report to HHS any transfers of value to physicians and teaching hospitals, and information on physician ownership or investment interests in the manufacturer.
It restores the prior law as if the health care law had never enacted those provisions, effective retroactively.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers would bear the cost: a physician who owns a hospital has a financial stake in sending patients there, which independent research has linked to higher use of imaging and services and higher Medicare spending. Patients would also lose the public database showing whether their doctor takes money from drug and device companies.

drawbacks.text: Physician-owned hospitals argue they offer specialized, efficient care and that the health care law's grandfathering freeze prevents new competitors from entering the market, a genuine cost an honest supporter could cite.
The Sunshine Act reporting requirement does impose real compliance paperwork on manufacturers, which the bill would eliminate.
Repealing the provisions retroactively, to the day the health care law was enacted, would unwind compliance steps hospitals and manufacturers had already taken.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver concrete gains to two narrow groups — physician-investors in specialty hospitals and manufacturers — while taking away two safeguards that mainly benefit patients and Medicare's finances. The paperwork burden on manufacturers is real but modest relative to the loss of transparency, and making the repeal retroactive would add disruption. On balance, the costs to patients and taxpayers outweigh the benefits to the industries.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late May 2010, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and sent to a health subcommittee on June 1 — and nothing further happened before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Doc Hastings introduced the bill on May 27, 2010 with four original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
On June 1, 2010 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; the record shows no markup, committee vote, or floor action afterward.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 without the bill receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients and Medicare kept the limits on physician self-referral to physician-owned hospitals and the public reporting of industry payments to doctors. Physician-owned hospital investors and drug and device manufacturers lost their chance at repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and Medicare; the repeal backers lost

for.name: Rep. Doc Hastings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the physician-owned hospital limits and the payment transparency requirements.

for.name: 5 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none advanced it beyond introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to its Health Subcommittee, and never reported it out.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All identified supporters — the sponsor and every cosponsor — were Republicans, while the Democratic majority controlled both committees that held the bill without action.

industries.note: Repealing the health care law's limits would let physician-investors expand hospitals they own and refer their Medicare patients to them, a conflict of interest linked to higher utilization and Medicare spending. Patients and taxpayers would absorb those costs.

industries.industry: Drug, device, biological, and medical supply manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would exempt manufacturers from reporting payments to physicians and physician ownership stakes to HHS, removing the public's visibility into financial ties between doctors and industry.
